title: York Play
description: The York Corpus Christi cycle: forty-eight (originally more) pageants dramatizing sacred history from the fall of Lucifer to the Last Judgement, performed annually by the city's craft guilds on wagons through the streets of York from the late fourteenth century to 1569. The longest and most complete surviving mystery cycle, registered in the great civic manuscript of 1463–77.
plot_or_argument: The cycle moves from the creation and fall of the angels, through the Old Testament pageants (Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Moses), to the life of Christ — the Annunciation, Nativity, ministry, the great Passion sequence (the Crucifixion and the death of Christ are its summit), the Harrowing of Hell, and the Resurrection — and closes with the Last Judgement.
narrative_structure: A sequential pageant cycle performed on Corpus Christi day, each play assigned to a guild (the Shipwrights' Noah, the Pinners' Crucifixion), the whole forming a civic salvation history.
principal_characters: God; Lucifer; Adam and Eve; Noah; Abraham; the Virgin Mary; Christ; Pilate; Herod; the soldiers of the Crucifixion
meter_and_prosody: Thirteen-line stanza and couplet forms, with the alliterative 'York realism' of the Passion pageants.
historical_context: The play is first mentioned in 1376, and the surviving register (BL Additional MS 35290) was compiled 1463–77; performances continued until suppressed in 1569, the cycle's long life making York the best-documented of the English civic dramas.
literary_significance: The greatest surviving English mystery cycle: its Passion sequence is among the most powerful religious writing of the Middle Ages, and its civic organization is the fullest expression of medieval urban piety.
attribution_notes: Collaborative (many guild poets, revised over generations); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MS 35290 (Register). Standard edition: R. Beadle, EETS SS 23–24 (2009–13).

title: Towneley Plays
description: The Towneley (Wakefield) cycle of thirty-two plays, from the Creation to the Last Judgement, preserved in the Towneley manuscript (c. 1500) and long associated with Wakefield: famous above all for the six plays in the nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' attributed to the Wakefield Master — including the Second Shepherds' Play, the comic masterpiece of the English cycles, with its sheep-stealing Mak and its nativity of the stolen lamb.
plot_or_argument: The cycle retells salvation history from Lucifer's fall through the patriarchs to Christ's Passion and the Judgement; the Master's plays — Noah and his scolding wife, the two Shepherds' plays, Herod, and the Buffeting — transform the biblical matter with a vernacular comedy of Yorkshire shepherds, shrews, and ranting tyrants unmatched in the other cycles.
narrative_structure: A pageant cycle of thirty-two plays, partially dependent on York but transformed by the Wakefield Master's comic and homiletic genius.
principal_characters: Mak the sheep-stealer; Gill; the shepherds (Coll, Gib, Daw); Noah and his wife; Herod; Christ; Pilate
meter_and_prosody: The unique nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' (aabcccbddb with internal rhyme) in the Master's plays; thirteen-line stanza and couplets elsewhere.
historical_context: Composed and compiled c. 1400–1500, probably at Wakefield, where the plays were performed on Corpus Christi day; the manuscript (Huntington Library, MS HM 1) belonged to the Towneley family of Lancashire, from which the cycle takes its name.
literary_significance: The Second Shepherds' Play is the most famous English medieval drama: the cycle's blend of farce and nativity embodies the mystery tradition at its theatrical summit.
attribution_notes: Collaborative; the 'Wakefield Master' is a scholarly construct for the author of the six stanza-linked plays.
bibliographical_notes: Huntington Library, MS HM 1. Standard edition: M. Stevens and A. C. Cawley, EETS SS 13–14 (1994).

title: N-Town Plays
description: A cycle of forty-two plays compiled in East Anglia in the second half of the fifteenth century, so called because its banns announce performance 'in N-town' — the name to be supplied by whatever town staged it. Its distinctive compilation includes a Passion play of great elaboration (the Mary Play tradition), the Parliament of Heaven, and the trial of Joseph and Mary, with a strong Marian and doctrinal emphasis.
plot_or_argument: From the Parliament of Heaven and the fall of Lucifer, the cycle moves through the Old Testament, the life of the Virgin (her conception, presentation, and betrothal, the trial of Joseph and Mary), the Nativity, the ministry and Passion — with its long two-part Passion sequence — to the Resurrection, the Assumption, and the Last Judgement.
narrative_structure: A compilation cycle: some pageants written for the cycle, others (the Mary Play, the Passion Play) incorporated from self-standing East Anglian dramas, under a general prologue claiming the N-town staging.
principal_characters: God; the Virgin Mary; Joseph; Christ; Pilate; Satan; the Prolocutor
meter_and_prosody: Thirteen-line and eight-line stanza forms, with the rime couée of the incorporated plays.
historical_context: Compiled c. 1468–1500 in East Anglia (perhaps at Bury St Edmunds or Thetford), in the devotional culture that produced Bokenham and Capgrave; preserved in BL Cotton MS Vespasian D.viii.
literary_significance: The most learned and Mariological of the cycles, and the principal witness to the East Anglian Passion play tradition; its compilation shows the cycle form in the making.
attribution_notes: Collaborative (compilational); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Vespasian D.viii. Standard edition: S. Spector, EETS SS 11–12 (1991).

title: Chester Mystery Plays
description: The Chester cycle of twenty-four plays, from the fall of Lucifer to the Last Judgement, performed at Whitsun by the guilds of Chester from the early fifteenth century (with later tradition dating its origin to the fourteenth) until 1575, the last of the great cycles to be suppressed. Its eight-line stanza, its Expositor figure, and its homiletic restraint give it a distinctive ceremonial gravity.
plot_or_argument: The cycle dramatizes salvation history in twenty-four pageants — the Creation and fall, Noah's flood (with the famous drinking-song of Noah's wife), Abraham and Isaac, the Prophets, the Nativity, the ministry, the Passion, the Harrowing of Hell, and the Last Judgement — with the Expositor commenting on the action's prophetic meaning.
narrative_structure: Twenty-four pageants on the Corpus Christi model, with the Expositor's speeches linking the Old Testament type to its New Testament fulfilment.
principal_characters: God; Lucifer; Adam and Eve; Noah and his wife; Abraham and Isaac; the Virgin Mary; Christ; Antichrist; the Expositor
meter_and_prosody: The characteristic Chester stanza (aaabcccb, with internal rhyme) and the Expositor's couplets.
historical_context: Performed at Whitsun in Chester from at least the early fifteenth century (a fourteenth-century origin is traditional), revised in the early sixteenth century, and performed until 1575; preserved in five manuscripts and printed in 1607.
literary_significance: The last surviving performance tradition of the English cycles (revived at Chester from 1951), and a classic of English civic theatre.
attribution_notes: Collaborative; the tradition attributing the cycle's origin to the monk Ranulph Higden is legendary.
bibliographical_notes: Five manuscripts (incl. BL Harley MS 2124). Standard edition: R. M. Lumiansky and D. Mills, EETS SS 3, 9 (1974–86).

title: The Castle of Perseverance
description: The earliest complete English morality play (c. 1400–25, 3,649 lines): the life of Mankind (Humanum Genus) from birth to judgement, staged on the famous circular 'place' with its central castle and five scaffolds, as the virtues and vices battle for his soul through the Seven Ages. The most ambitious play of the English medieval stage.
plot_or_argument: Mankind, born in sin, is led by his Bad Angel through World, Flesh, and the Devil to the seven deadly sins; rescued by Confession, he is garrisoned in the Castle of Perseverance with the virtues; the sins' siege fails, but Covetousness wins him in old age, until Death strikes and the debate of the four daughters of God — Mercy, Peace, Righteousness, Truth — yields his salvation.
narrative_structure: A four-scaffold cosmic drama (God; World; Flesh; Devil) around the central castle, with the banns, the siege, the death scene, and the parliament of heaven as its great movements.
principal_characters: Mankind (Humanum Genus); the Bad and Good Angels; World, Flesh, and the Devil; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Seven Virtues; Confession; Death; God; the Four Daughters of God
meter_and_prosody: Thirteen-line stanzas (rime couée with wheel), with stage directions prescribing the elaborate fixed staging.
historical_context: Composed c. 1400–25 in East Anglia (the manuscript's language is Norfolk), in the milieu of the great fifteenth-century moralities; preserved uniquely in the Macro manuscript (Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354, c. 1440) with Mankind and Wisdom.
literary_significance: The foundational English morality: its stage diagram, its allegorical cast, and its theology of mercy set the pattern for the genre through Everyman to the Elizabethan stage.
bibliographical_notes: Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354 (Macro). Standard edition: M. Eccles, The Macro Plays, EETS OS 262 (1969); D. N. Klausner, TEAMS (2010).

title: Mankind
description: The liveliest of the English moralities (c. 1465–70): the comedy of Mankind, the East Anglian farmer, tempted from his spade and his beads by Mischief, New Guise, Nowadays, and Nought, and the devil Titivillus, whose whispered discouragements drive him to despair — until Mercy reclaims him. Famous for its scatological comedy and its collection of money from the audience, it shows the morality in its most theatrical form.
plot_or_argument: Mercy instructs Mankind in labour and prayer; the vice-companions tempt him to idleness and lechery; the devil Titivillus, appearing under the stage, whispers despair and steals his devotion; Mankind falls, is saved from suicide by Mercy's return, and repents, beating off the vices with his spade.
narrative_structure: A compact morality of temptation, fall, and mercy, in the alternating mode of sermon and farce, with direct address and the audience collection ('Now gostly to our purpose') as its signature.
principal_characters: Mankind; Mercy; Mischief; New Guise; Nowadays; Nought; Titivillus
meter_and_prosody: Couplets, stanza forms, and the macaronic dog-Latin of the vices, with remarkable metrical variety.
historical_context: Composed c. 1465–70 in East Anglia (Cambridgeshire/Norfolk), for performance by a travelling company; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354).
literary_significance: The most theatrical of the moralities and a key witness to professional playing in the fifteenth century; its Titivillus and audience games bridge medieval and Tudor comedy.
bibliographical_notes: Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354 (Macro). Standard edition: M. Eccles, The Macro Plays, EETS OS 262 (1969); in Everyman and Mankind, Arden Early Modern Drama (2009).

title: Wisdom
description: The most learned and musical of the English moralities (c. 1460–70): the play of the soul — Mind, Will, and Understanding — wedded to Wisdom (Christ), corrupted by Lucifer into a life of lechery and law, and reclaimed through penance. Its elaborate costumes, dances, and liturgical music suggest performance by a learned monastic or clerical household.
plot_or_argument: Wisdom (Christ) espouses the soul with her powers Mind, Will, and Understanding; Lucifer tempts them to abandon contemplation for the world, and the soul falls into lechery, maintenance of law, and perjury; Wisdom returns, and the powers, moved by his speeches, do penance and are restored to grace.
narrative_structure: A two-movement morality (union with Wisdom; fall and restoration), with the masque-like dances and the court of Lucifer as its theatrical centre.
principal_characters: Wisdom (Christ); Anima (the Soul); Mind; Will; Understanding; Lucifer; the Seven Deadly Sins
meter_and_prosody: Stanza forms with Latin liturgical texts and music cues, the most literate of the moralities.
historical_context: Composed c. 1460–70, probably for an East Anglian monastic or noble household with trained singers; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354) and Bodleian Digby MS 133.
literary_significance: The most theologically sophisticated English morality: its fusion of mystical doctrine, music, and dance makes it a summit of the genre's learned tradition.
bibliographical_notes: Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354 (Macro). Standard edition: M. Eccles, The Macro Plays, EETS OS 262 (1969).

title: Everyman
description: The most famous of the English moralities, translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) around 1500: Everyman, summoned by Death to render his account, finds that Fellowship, Kindred, Goods, and even his own Strength and Beauty desert him, and that only Good Deeds — and Knowledge, Confession, and the priesthood — go with him into the grave. Its stark allegory of death has kept it on the stage for five centuries.
plot_or_argument: God, seeing mankind sunk in worldly love, sends Death to Everyman with the summons to his reckoning; one by one his companions refuse the journey — Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin, Goods — until Good Deeds, weakened by his neglect, sends him to Knowledge, who leads him through Confession and penance to the sacraments; at the grave, Strength, Discretion, Beauty, and the Five Wits desert him in turn, and only Good Deeds descends with him, as the angels receive his soul.
narrative_structure: A single-movement morality of the final journey, with the successive desertions of the companions as its pitiless rhythm and the doctrine of the reckoning as its frame.
principal_characters: Everyman; Death; God; Fellowship; Kindred; Cousin; Goods; Good Deeds; Knowledge; Confession; Strength; Discretion; Beauty; the Five Wits; the Angel; the Doctor
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and stanza forms, plain and weighty, with the Dutch original's structure faithfully kept.
historical_context: Translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) c. 1500 and printed by Richard Pynson and John Skot c. 1510–1535; continuously performed since, including modern productions (Hofmannsthal's Jedermann at Salzburg descends from it).
literary_significance: The classic English play of death and the reckoning: its allegory has made it the most performed medieval English drama in the modern world.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; translated from the Dutch, whose authorship is likewise disputed.
bibliographical_notes: Four early prints (c. 1510–35). Standard editions: in Everyman and Mankind, Arden Early Modern Drama (2009); A. C. Cawley (1961).

title: Croxton Play of the Sacrament
description: An East Anglian miracle play of c. 1461 on the host: the Jewish merchant Jonathas and his fellows buy the consecrated wafer from the Christian merchant Aristorius, subject it to their tests — and when they stab it, it bleeds, and the image of Christ appears, converting them all. Its staging directions (the cauldron, the severed hand, the miraculous oven) make it the most spectacular of the English miracle plays.
plot_or_argument: Aristorius, tempted by gold, sells the host to Jonathas, who with his companions proves it in their own body of tests: boiling, oven, and dagger; the host bleeds, sticks to Jonathas's hand, and the image of Christ as a child reproves them; their conversion follows, the church is reconciled, and the play ends with the doctor's epilogue and the procession.
narrative_structure: A two-part miracle (the bargain and the testing; the miracle and conversion), framed by the banns and the closing sermon.
principal_characters: Jonathas; Aristorius the merchant; the priest Isoder; the Jews Jason, Jasdon, Masphat, Malchus; the Bishop; the Image of Christ
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and stanza forms, with stage directions prescribing spectacular effects.
historical_context: Composed c. 1461 at Croxton, Norfolk (the banns name the village), when the cult of the host and the Corpus Christi confraternities flourished; its treatment of Jews reflects the period's anti-Judaism, and its conversion plot the theology of eucharistic miracle; preserved in Trinity College, Dublin, MS F.4.20.
literary_significance: The fullest English miracle play and the most spectacular document of the late medieval eucharistic cult; its staging is central to the history of English theatre.
bibliographical_notes: Trinity College, Dublin, MS F.4.20. Standard edition: N. Davis, EETS OS 262 (1970); G. L. Aiken, TEAMS (2019).

title: Digby Mary Magdalene
alternative_titles: The Digby Play of Mary Magdalene
description: The most ambitious of the English saints' plays (c. 1480–1500, 2,139 lines): the life of Mary Magdalene from her worldly grandeur and conversion through her apostolate in Marseilles to her thirty years as a desert hermit fed by angels. Its multiple locations, ship voyages, and spectacular effects make it the fullest surviving English drama of a female saint.
plot_or_argument: Mary, the proud lady of Magdalene castle, falls into lechery; Christ's grace converts her, and after the Passion she sails to Marseilles, converts the king and queen, raises the queen from death, and converts the pagan priest; retiring to the wilderness, she is fed by angels, receives the last rites, and her soul is borne to heaven.
narrative_structure: A multi-location saint's play in the continental manner, moving between Jerusalem, Marseilles, and the wilderness, with ships, temple, and heaven's scaffolds.
principal_characters: Mary Magdalene; Christ; the King and Queen of Marseilles; the pagan priest; the angels; the devils
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and stanza forms, with macaronic Latin in the liturgical scenes.
historical_context: Composed c. 1480–1500 in East Anglia, in the flourishing of the Mary Magdalene cult; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 133 (c. 1512), with The Conversion of St Paul and the morality Wisdom.
literary_significance: The fullest English female saint's play and the most elaborately staged of the East Anglian dramas; its conversion and travel plot is a summit of the miracle play tradition.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, Digby MS 133. Standard edition: D. C. Baker, J. L. Murphy, and L. B. Hall, EETS OS 283 (1982); T. Coletti, TEAMS (2018).
